## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Durājānajātaka* (Ja 64) is a short narrative in the Pali *Jātaka* collection. According to the commentary edited by V. Fausböll, the Buddha delivered the story while residing at Jetavana about a devout lay follower (*upāsaka*) of Sāvatthi who was established in the Three Refuges and the five precepts [Fausböll 1877]. The man's wife was immoral and fickle: on days when she committed adultery, she behaved meekly like a purchased slave-girl, but on days when she did not, she acted tyrannical and arrogant, leaving her confused husband so distressed that he ceased visiting the Buddha [Fausböll 1877].

Addressing the layman's bewilderment regarding the unpredictable nature of women, the Buddha recounted the past story, opening with the verse *Mā su nandi icchati man ti* [Fausböll 1877]. Hearing the exposition of the truths, the lay disciple attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*), while the wife, realizing the Buddha was fully aware of her misbehavior, abandoned her evil ways [Fausböll 1877]. In the birth-story identification (*samodhāna*), the Buddha revealed that the husband and wife of the past were the very same couple, and he himself had been their teacher (*ācariya*) [Fausböll 1877].
